title: Network Delay Time
description: Brute force to optimized: Bellman-Ford relaxing every edge repeatedly versus Dijkstra's greedy nearest-node algorithm.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given n nodes and a list of directed, weighted edges times = [source, target, weight] (travel time), and a starting node k, return the time it takes for a signal starting at k to reach ALL nodes, or -1 if some node is unreachable.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","times (weighted directed edges), n, k"],["Output","The maximum shortest travel time to any node, or -1 if unreachable"],["Key Insight","This is a single-source shortest path problem; the answer is the MAXIMUM shortest distance across all nodes"],["Constraints","Up to 100 nodes, non-negative weights"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Weighted edges, single source, find shortest time to reach every node\"","A classic single-source shortest path problem, solved efficiently with Dijkstra's algorithm since all weights are non-negative"]]}

blocks.text: This is directly Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm from a single source node k. Compute the shortest distance from k to every other node; if any node remains unreachable (infinite distance), return -1. Otherwise, the answer is the MAXIMUM of these shortest distances, since the signal only "fully" reaches all nodes once even the FARTHEST one receives it.

blocks.title: Analogy: How Long Until a Message Reaches the Last Person in a Relay Network
blocks.text: Picture a message broadcast from one person through a network of relays with varying transmission delays. The time until EVERYONE has received the message is determined by whoever is slowest to receive it, the person with the LONGEST shortest-path delay from the original sender.

blocks.caption: Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest distances from k; the answer is the maximum across all nodes

blocks.text: Result: 2 (node 2 reaches 1 and 3 in 1 minute, then 3 reaches 4 in 1 more minute, total 2).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Initialize the distance to the source k as 0, and every other node as infinity (unknown/unreached).

Observation 2: Repeatedly select the UNVISITED node with the smallest currently known distance (this greedy choice is always safe since all weights are non-negative), mark it visited, and RELAX all of its outgoing edges (update a neighbor's distance if reaching it through the current node is shorter than previously known).

Observation 3: Repeating this process n times (once per node) correctly finalizes every node's true shortest distance from k.

Observation 4: After the algorithm completes, if any node's distance remains infinity, it is unreachable, return -1; otherwise, the answer is the MAXIMUM distance found across all nodes.
This leads to running Dijkstra's algorithm from k, then taking the maximum of the resulting shortest distances.
Use the Bellman-Ford algorithm instead: relax every single edge, repeated n-1 times, gradually converging to the correct shortest distances (works even with negative weights, though not needed here).
Why the code is written this way

items: Relaxing every edge repeatedly correctly converges to shortest distances, working even with negative weights.
This costs O(n times edges), more than needed since all weights here are guaranteed non-negative; Dijkstra's algorithm exploits this guarantee for better efficiency.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times edges) for Bellman-Ford.
Space: O(n) for the distance array.
Limitation: Dijkstra's algorithm, exploiting the non-negative weight guarantee, achieves better time complexity using a greedy nearest-node selection strategy.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build an adjacency list from times. Initialize dist[k] = 0, all other distances to infinity, and a visited array all false. Repeat n times: find the UNVISITED node with the smallest current distance; if none remains reachable, stop early. Mark it visited, then relax every outgoing edge from it (updating a neighbor's distance if a shorter path is found through the current node). After the loop, if any node's distance is still infinity, return -1; otherwise return the maximum distance found.
Use Dijkstra's algorithm: repeatedly expand the closest unvisited node, relaxing its outgoing edges.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Action"],"rows":[["dist[2]=0","starting node"],["Expand 2","relax edges to 1 (dist=1) and 3 (dist=1)"],["Expand 1 or 3 (tie, dist=1)","expand 3, relax edge to 4 (dist=2)"],["Expand remaining nodes","no further improvements; max distance is 2"]]}

blocks.text: Since all edge weights are non-negative, greedily always expanding the currently closest unvisited node guarantees that once a node is marked visited, its recorded distance is ALREADY its true shortest distance (a later, longer path could never improve upon it, since all weights only add non-negative amounts); relaxing every outgoing edge from each expanded node correctly propagates improvements to its neighbors, and after all reachable nodes are processed, the maximum distance found is exactly when the "slowest" node finally receives the signal.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) with this simple array-based implementation (improvable to O((n plus edges) log n) with a priority queue).
Space: O(n plus edges) for the adjacency list.

blocks.text: Network Delay Time is a direct, practical application of single-source shortest path algorithms, specifically highlighting when Dijkstra's greedy approach is valid (non-negative weights).

items: Using Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with NEGATIVE weights, where its greedy assumption breaks down (Bellman-Ford would be required instead).
Forgetting to take the MAXIMUM of the final distances, instead mistakenly summing them or returning some other combination.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "shortest time for a signal to reach all nodes, non-negative weighted edges", think: Dijkstra's algorithm, then take the maximum shortest distance.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Bellman-Ford costs O(n times edges); Dijkstra's algorithm costs O(n squared) with a simple array (or O((n plus edges) log n) with a heap), the standard efficient solution for non-negative weights.

items: Pattern: single-source shortest path via Dijkstra's algorithm.
Core Idea: greedily expand the closest unvisited node, relaxing its outgoing edges; the answer is the maximum shortest distance across all nodes.
Time: O(n times edges) for Bellman-Ford, O(n squared) (or better with a heap) for Dijkstra's algorithm.
Most Important Observation: Dijkstra's greedy nearest-node strategy is valid ONLY because all weights are non-negative.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, foundational medium-level weighted shortest-path problem.
One line memory trick: Dijkstra from k, then take the max distance.
